people.name: Teferi Fufa
body: In early September 1972 a young Oromo man arrived in Minnesota by himself to start college. Teferi Fufa enrolled at Bethel College in Arden Hills, planning to get an education and go home to serve his country. A few weeks earlier another Oromo student, Tasissa Moti, had arrived with his American wife, Geri. That Christmas, two Oromo immigrants celebrated together in Minnesota, a moment MNopedia's chronology marks as the beginning of an Oromo community in the state.

Fufa later transferred to the University of Minnesota. Then events at home changed his plans. By his MNopedia biography, conditions in Ethiopia kept getting worse even after a change of government, so he became a U.S. citizen and stayed. He went on to a career as an educator and, as of that biography, is retired and working on peace and equity causes in the United States and abroad.

As refugees began arriving in the 1980s, the small student group grew. By the middle of that decade more than 200 Oromo people lived in the Twin Cities. Oromo Minnesotans founded the Oromo Relief Association of North America in 1981 to help refugees in camps and find American sponsor families, and in April 1982 they took part in St. Paul's Festival of Nations for the first time, displaying the Oromo flag among those of more than a hundred nations.

Fufa's later contribution is as a historian of that community. He wrote MNopedia's article "Oromos in Minnesota: The Making of Little Oromia," published by the Minnesota Historical Society in 2021, and photographs from his personal collection illustrate it. MNopedia describes him as one of the first two Oromos to settle in Minnesota.
keyFacts: September 1972: Arrives in Minnesota to attend Bethel College in Arden Hills, later transferring to the University of Minnesota.
Becomes a U.S. citizen and stays in Minnesota as conditions in Ethiopia worsen; now a retired educator.
February 16, 2021: MNopedia publishes his article on Oromo history in Minnesota.
His personal collection supplied MNopedia's photographs of early community life, including a 1984 social gathering in a Twin Cities home.

people.name: Tashitaa Tufaa
body: Every school day, thousands of Minnesota children climb onto buses run by a company that began with one van, the one belonging to Tashitaa Tufaa's wife. Tufaa and his brother started the business in the early 2000s. It grew into Metropolitan Transportation Network (MTN), based in Fridley. Voice of America dates the start to 2003, and School Bus Fleet to 2004.

Tufaa grew up in the Oromia region of Ethiopia, working on his family's farm with 13 brothers and sisters, and later became a schoolteacher. He campaigned for a party that opposed Ethiopia's ruling coalition. When he no longer felt safe, he left the country, and he came to the United States as a refugee in 1992.

His first jobs were dishwashing, manufacturing and security work. He then drove for Metro Mobility, carrying older adults and people with disabilities, and later drove a cab. That work taught him the transportation business from the driver's seat.

In 2017 Voice of America reported that MTN had almost 300 buses and vans and more than 300 employees. School Bus Fleet described more than 300 vehicles, over 400 employees and about 15,000 K-12 students carried each day across the Twin Cities. Voice of America also reported that since 2012 three former employees had started their own transportation companies.

He has also backed other community efforts. In 2021 Sahan Journal reported that he chaired the board of Oromia 11, a new television network in downtown Minneapolis, and in 2022 it named him as a fundraising mentor to congressional candidate Amane Badhasso.
keyFacts: 1992: Arrives in the United States as a refugee, after working as a schoolteacher in Ethiopia.
Drives for Metro Mobility, then a cab.
2003 or 2004: Founds MTN with his brother, depending on the source.
2017: About 15,000 students carried each day, by School Bus Fleet's count.
Since 2012: Three former employees have launched their own transportation companies.

people.name: Amane Badhasso
body: In summer 2022, a 32-year-old first-time candidate in St. Paul raised more than $800,000 to challenge the longtime incumbent U.S. representative in the DFL primary for Minnesota's Fourth Congressional District. Had she won, Sahan Journal noted, Amane Badhasso would have been the first Oromo to serve in Congress.

Badhasso was born into a farming family in an Ethiopian village and was raised for a time in the city of Asella by extended family. When she was about five, she moved with her father and 13 siblings to a refugee camp in Kenya. After the U.S. initially denied the family's resettlement case, they left the camp and lived for about eight years in urban neighborhoods in Kenya. She arrived in Minnesota at 13 and grew up in St. Paul.

She studied political science at Hamline University, graduating in 2015. She interned for the DFL in 2011, worked on a Fifth District congressional campaign from 2013 to 2015, organized for a 2019 St. Paul City Council campaign and worked on a 2020 legislative campaign. She also served as president of the International Oromo Youth Association and worked as a researcher for a compliance firm in Washington, D.C.
On August 9, 2022, the incumbent won the primary with 83.4 percent of the vote to Badhasso's 15.2 percent, according to the University of Minnesota's election archive.
keyFacts: Went to a Kenyan refugee camp at about age five; lived about eight years in Kenya after an initial U.S. denial.
Moved to Minnesota at age 13.
2015: B.A. in political science, Hamline University.
Served as president of the International Oromo Youth Association.
August 9, 2022: Lost the DFL primary for the Fourth District to the incumbent U.S. representative, 83.4 percent to 15.2 percent.

people.name: Asafa Jalata
body: For more than three decades, students at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, have learned about Indigenous rights, nationalism and global inequality from a sociologist who places the Oromo experience alongside that of other colonized peoples. In 2023 the university's College of Arts and Sciences recognized Asafa Jalata's 32 years on the sociology faculty by naming him the Betty Lynn Hendrickson Professor.

Jalata earned his Ph.D. at the State University of New York at Binghamton in 1990, the year MNopedia gives for the formation of the Oromo Studies Association. His books include Contending Nationalisms of Oromia and Ethiopia (2010) and The Oromo Movement and Imperial Politics (2021). The university credits him with 15 books and more than 70 peer-reviewed articles, chapters and works of public sociology.

He has also built institutions for his field. He has served as president of the Oromo Studies Association, which gave him its Lifetime Achievement Award in 2020, and he has edited the Journal of Oromo Studies. He also writes for general readers, with seven articles at The Conversation.
keyFacts: 1990: Ph.D., SUNY Binghamton.
32 years on the UT Knoxville sociology faculty as of 2023.
Professor of Sociology and Global and Africana Studies.
Former president of the Oromo Studies Association and editor of the Journal of Oromo Studies.
2020: Oromo Studies Association Lifetime Achievement Award.
2023: Named Betty Lynn Hendrickson Professor.

people.name: Mohammed Hassen
body: In 1983, a doctoral thesis at the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London, took on the question of who the Oromo were and when they became part of Ethiopia's history. Mohammed Hassen's thesis, "The Oromo of Ethiopia, 1500–1850," became the basis of a book. Cambridge University Press published The Oromo of Ethiopia: A History, 1570–1860 in 1990.

He taught at Georgia State University in Atlanta, where the Department of History now lists him as an emeritus associate professor under the name Mohammed Hassen Ali. His teaching covered world civilization and the history of Eastern, Central and Southern Africa, and his research centered on the history of the Oromo people of Ethiopia.

His later book, The Oromo and the Christian Kingdom of Ethiopia, 1300–1700 (James Currey, 2015), argues that the Oromo were "neither foreigners nor newcomers to Ethiopia" and have been part of its native population since at least the early 1300s. The argument bears on whether the Oromo are seen as rightful inhabitants of their homeland.
Hassen has also served as a contributing editor of the Journal of Oromo Studies and The Horn of Africa.
keyFacts: 1983: Ph.D., SOAS, University of London.
1990: The Oromo of Ethiopia: A History, 1570–1860 (Cambridge University Press).
2015: The Oromo and the Christian Kingdom of Ethiopia, 1300–1700 (James Currey).
Emeritus associate professor of history, Georgia State University.

people.name: Gemechis Desta Buba
body: In the early 2000s, Gemechis Desta Buba, ordained in 2001, was pastor of St. Stephen Evangelical Lutheran Church and the African/Oromo Lutheran Church in Atlanta. Originally from Ethiopia, he studied at Mekane Yesus Theological Seminary, where he later taught, and at the Interdenominational Theological Center in Atlanta.

He earned a doctorate in missional leadership from Columbia Theological Seminary in 2006 and became Director of African National Ministries in the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America. By his Day1 biography, he has also served as president of the worldwide union of Oromo Evangelical Churches and as an assistant to the bishop of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Synod.

He later led international missions for the North American Lutheran Church as an assistant to the bishop. The church reported in 2023 that he would serve part time from Ethiopia while expanding his teaching and leadership work worldwide. Nothing more recent about his role was found.

In Minnesota, Christian Oromos began a prayer and Bible study group in the 1980s that in 1993 became Our Redeemer Oromo Evangelical Church in Minneapolis, according to MNopedia. Muslim Oromos opened Masjid Tawfiq in Minneapolis in 2004, which MNopedia calls the first Oromo mosque in North America.
keyFacts: 2001: Ordained.
2006: Doctorate in missional leadership, Columbia Theological Seminary.
Served as Director of African National Ministries, Evangelical Lutheran Church in America.
Served as president of the worldwide union of Oromo Evangelical Churches.
2023: Began serving the North American Lutheran Church part time from Ethiopia, by the church's report.

people.name: Ezekiel Gebissa
body: In 2003, a history professor at Kettering University in Flint, Michigan, a school best known for engineering, went to Ethiopia as a Fulbright Scholar at Addis Ababa University for the 2003–2004 academic year. Ezekiel Gebissa had earned a bachelor's degree at Addis Ababa University in 1984, and a master's and a Ph.D. at Michigan State University in 1991 and 1997.

Gebissa studies khat, a stimulant leaf chewed socially in parts of East Africa and restricted under U.S. drug law. His book Leaf of Allah: Khat and Agricultural Transformation in Harerge, Ethiopia, 1875–1991 (2004) examines how khat changed farming and the economy in the eastern region of Harerge. He also edited Taking the Place of Food: Khat in Ethiopia (2010).

He has served as editor-in-chief of the Journal of Oromo Studies and edited Contested Terrain: Essays on Oromo Studies, Ethiopianist Discourses, and Politically Engaged Scholarship (Red Sea Press, 2009). Kettering's directory now lists him as a professor of social science in its School of Foundational Studies, with a specialization in African history.

2003–2004: Fulbright U.S. Scholar in history at Addis Ababa University.

Has served as editor-in-chief of the Journal of Oromo Studies.

people.name: Mohammed Ademo
body: While living in the United States, a young Oromo journalist started a website so that news about his community could be told from within it. Mohammed Ademo founded and edited OPride, an independent news site about the Oromo and Ethiopia. He also worked as an editor at Al Jazeera America and wrote for Foreign Policy.
Ademo has written for Minnesota readers in Sahan Journal, including a 2020 story on the Oromo Witness book and a 2022 piece on a documentary about the singer Haacaaluu Hundeessaa.

After 16 years in the United States, he moved to Ethiopia and was appointed director of the Oromia Broadcasting Network in October 2018. In February 2019, The Reporter Ethiopia reported that he had been replaced. He told the paper he had not resigned and that the government wanted to go in a different direction; the network's board chair said the government wanted to give him a better assignment. OPride's own notice says the site stopped operating in September 2018, and it now stands as an archive.
keyFacts: Founder and editor of OPride; the site ceased operations in September 2018.
Former editor at Al Jazeera America.
Contributor to Sahan Journal, 2020 and 2022.

people.name: Tasissa Moti
people.dates: Birth and death years not published
body: In late August 1972, Tasissa Moti arrived in Minnesota as a student with his American wife, Geri, a nurse who had served as a missionary in Ethiopia. He studied at a community college in Minneapolis and later transferred to the University of Minnesota. A few weeks after he arrived, Teferi Fufa came to study at Bethel College. That Christmas, two Oromo immigrants celebrated together in Minnesota, which MNopedia's chronology records as the start of the Oromo community in the state.

Before the refugee arrivals of the 1980s and 1990s, a handful of students, and in Moti's case a marriage, linked Ethiopia and the Upper Midwest. Within about a decade Oromo Minnesotans had founded the Oromo Relief Association of North America, and agencies such as Lutheran Social Service, Lutheran World Relief and the International Institute of Minnesota helped move refugees from camps to sponsor families in the Twin Cities. MNopedia is the only account of Moti found.
keyFacts: Late August 1972: Arrives in Minnesota as a student with his wife, Geri.
Studies at a Minneapolis community college, then transfers to the University of Minnesota.
Christmas 1972: Two Oromo immigrants celebrate together, recorded by MNopedia as the start of the Oromo community in Minnesota.
1981: The Oromo Relief Association of North America is founded in the Twin Cities.

people.name: Gebisa Ejeta
body: On October 15, 2009, in Des Moines, Iowa, a Purdue University plant scientist received the World Food Prize, a private award of $250,000. Gebisa Ejeta was honored for sorghum hybrids that survive severe drought and resist Striga, a parasitic weed that can destroy whole harvests in Africa.

Ejeta was born in 1950 in the village of Wollonkomi in west-central Ethiopia. Purdue reports that as a boy he walked 12.5 miles to school on Sunday nights and walked home on Fridays. He earned a bachelor's degree in plant science from Alemaya College in eastern Ethiopia, then a master's degree in 1976 and a Ph.D. in 1978 at Purdue.

His sorghum hybrid, introduced in 1983 and scaled up with farmers' cooperatives in Sudan, yielded more than double what traditional varieties produced. A Striga-resistant variety followed in 1994. According to Purdue, his work has helped feed hundreds of millions of people in sub-Saharan Africa.

Ejeta also served in U.S. public life as a special advisor to the administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development, a State Department science envoy and a member of the Board for International Food and Agricultural Development. Purdue launched its Center for Global Food Security in 2011 with him at its head and named him a Presidential Fellow in 2022. He received the National Medal of Science in 2023 and joined the National Inventors Hall of Fame Class of 2026. Purdue says he retired in 2025 and lists him as Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Agronomy.

The biographies from Purdue, the Carnegie Corporation and the National Inventors Hall of Fame describe him as Ethiopian-born and name no ethnic group. He appears on this page because in 2009 he gave Voice of America's Afaan Oromo staff an interview, listed under the Oromo spelling of his name, Gabbisaa Ejjetaa. That does not show how he identifies.
keyFacts: 1950: Born in the village of Wollonkomi, west-central Ethiopia.
1976 and 1978: Master's degree and Ph.D., Purdue University.
1983: Drought-tolerant sorghum hybrid introduced; Striga-resistant variety follows in 1994.
2009: World Food Prize laureate.
2023: National Medal of Science.
2025: Retires from Purdue.
2026: National Inventors Hall of Fame.

people.name: Hangasu Waqo Lugo and Abdul Dire
people.field: History, oral history, community building, philanthropy
body: In August 2020, Abdul Dire released his first book, Oromo Witness; a photo caption in Sahan Journal mentions a release reading on August 15 in St. Paul. It tells the life of Hangasu Waqo Lugo, whom Sahan Journal describes as one of the few living first-hand witnesses to the Bale Oromo movement of 1963 to 1970, an armed uprising in the Bale region of southeastern Ethiopia. Dire recorded interviews with him from 2013 to 2020. The account is Hangasu's own memory.

By the publisher's account, Hangasu sat beside his father, Wako Lugo, from battlefield to negotiating table. Sahan Journal reports that he was born into a family of warriors, that as a teenager he met Emperor Haile Selassie and argued with him, and that he was imprisoned in Somalia after going to Mogadishu to seek support for the movement. The publisher adds that in the 1990s he ran for a parliamentary seat representing his home district. In 2000 he arrived in St. Paul as a refugee. Sahan Journal reports that in Minnesota he organizes the Oromo community, builds schools and sponsors young students, following the emphasis on education of his uncle, Waqo Gutu.

Sahan Journal describes Dire as a Minnesota-based tech leader and philanthropist and a descendant of the Bale resistance leaders. Mohammed Ademo, who wrote that story and whose grandfather died in the revolt, called these fighters "conspicuously absent from Ethiopian historiography."

Frederick Melo reviewed the book in the Saint Paul Pioneer Press, and the publisher displays a 2021 Independent Press Award silver seal. According to Flexible Press, most profits go to the Burqaa Guddinnaa Foundation, which works on Oromo children's identity and provides school supplies to students in need in Ethiopia. A foundation representative said more than 750 children had received supplies.
keyFacts: 1963–1970: Bale Oromo movement; by the publisher's account, Hangasu sat beside his father, Wako Lugo, from battlefield to negotiating table.
Imprisoned in Somalia after seeking support for the movement in Mogadishu.
2000: Hangasu comes to the United States as a refugee, per Sahan Journal.
2013–2020: Abdul Dire records interviews with him.
August 2020: Oromo Witness (Flexible Press) released; a release reading was held August 15 in St. Paul.
Most profits support the Burqaa Guddinnaa Foundation.

people.name: Seenaa Jimjimo
body: In 2018 the U.S. House of Representatives passed House Resolution 128, which called for respect for human rights and inclusive governance in Ethiopia. Seenaa Jimjimo, an Oromo American, is credited by both Just Security and her own organization as a key player in that effort.

Jimjimo was born and raised in Ethiopia and, by her biography, has advocated for Oromo people, especially women, from a young age. She studied political science as an undergraduate and public health and public administration in graduate school. At the University of Illinois she served as a senator at large for the Graduate Student Association and as treasurer of the African Student Organization, and she received the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Scholarship and the Whitney M. Young Fellowship.

She is executive director of the Oromo Legacy Leadership & Advocacy Association (OLLAA), a U.S. nonprofit that works mainly with Oromo-speaking communities. She has written on U.S. policy toward Ethiopia, including a September 28, 2020, essay in Just Security, a national-security law and policy journal. Just Security also notes that she works as an environmental health specialist.
keyFacts: Born and raised in Ethiopia; Oromo American.
2018: Credited as a key contributor to House Resolution 128 on human rights in Ethiopia.
Executive director of OLLAA.
September 28, 2020: "Ethiopian Democracy Veers Off Track: What's at Stake" in Just Security.

people.name: Teferi Nigussie Tafa
body: In 2016 UNESCO added the Gada system, the Oromo system of self-government built on classes that take turns holding authority, to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. OLLAA's board page credits Teferi Nigussie Tafa, an Oromo scholar in St. Paul who serves on that board, as instrumental in the inscription and in forming the Oromo Gada Council in 2014.

Tafa is an assistant professor at the University of Northwestern in St. Paul and a novelist and filmmaker. By OLLAA's account he holds a Ph.D. in literature from Addis Ababa University, has taught at Addis Ababa and Ambo universities and as a visiting professor at Norwich University, and published the first scholarly analysis of novels and films in the Oromo language.
He speaks publicly about Oromo culture in Minnesota. In an October 2025 Ampers segment on Irreechaa, he described the festival to American listeners as "Oromo Thanksgiving."

2016: UNESCO inscribes Gada; OLLAA credits him as instrumental.

people.name: Lokho Kotile
body: On August 9, 2025, six emerging Oromo artists showed their work for one night at the Oromo Community of Minnesota center in St. Paul. The exhibit, "Under the Odaa Tree," was curated by Lokho Kotile with community organizer Naima Badri. Kotile explained its name: the odaa, a sycamore that appears on the Oromo flag, is in her words "a hub for who the Oromo people are."

Kotile describes herself as a proud Oromo woman whose roots shape her themes of home, belonging and nature. She earned a Master of Fine Arts in visual studies from the Minneapolis College of Art and Design, focusing on illustration, photography and mixed-media storytelling. She has taught English as a second language to young learners and works as a middle school art teacher and reading interventionist. She founded Lokho's Lens, her studio and design practice.

Her own work uses watercolor and expressive movement to explore emotion. In April 2026 she held a solo exhibition, Lost in Abstraction, and she showed work in the 2026 group exhibition MARA, alongside the work of the singer Haacaaluu Hundeessaa and other Twin Cities artists.
keyFacts: Master of Fine Arts, Minneapolis College of Art and Design.
Teacher and writer.

institutions.name: Oromo Community of Minnesota
body: In the early 1980s, Oromo Minnesotans began meeting in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood of Minneapolis. That group became the Oromo Community of Minnesota. Its own website says it began as an informal mutual assistance association, was formally established in 1985 and received 501(c)(3) status in 2000.

A state CareerForce listing says the organization paid off the mortgage on its St. Paul center in 2013, and calls it the first African immigrant community to fully own a community building in Minnesota. The organization lists help with public benefits applications, immigration and naturalization, case management, health navigation and insurance enrollment, employment, and youth academic support and leadership. Its seniors program offers interpretation, transportation, home visits and help with clinic appointments.

The center also hosts arts and culture events. On August 9, 2025, it hosted "Under the Odaa Tree," with stipends and workshops for six emerging artists, music and dance by the Oromo Youth Association of Minnesota, and a traditional coffee ceremony.
keyFacts: Early 1980s: Group begins meeting in Cedar-Riverside, Minneapolis.
1985: Formally established, by its own account; 2000: 501(c)(3) status.
2013: Pays off the mortgage on its St. Paul center, per CareerForce.
Latest dated post on its website when checked: January 29, 2026.

institutions.name: Oromo Studies Association
institutions.dates: Established 1986 by its own account; MNopedia gives 1990
institutions.location: North America; 2026 annual conference in Minneapolis
body: The Oromo Studies Association grew out of papers presented at annual meetings of the Union of Oromo in North America, which, MNopedia notes, had a strong Minnesota chapter. The association's website says it was established in 1986; MNopedia dates its formation to 1990.

It is a multidisciplinary association that supports research on Oromo history, culture, politics, health and education. Since 1993 it has published the Journal of Oromo Studies, which is now fully open access. It holds two conferences a year. Its 2026 annual conference, "Oromos on the Global Landscape," met in Minneapolis from July 31 to August 2, 2026, in person and online.
keyFacts: 1986: Established, by its own account; MNopedia gives 1990.
1993: Journal of Oromo Studies begins publication; now open access.
July 31–August 2, 2026: Annual conference in Minneapolis.

institutions.name: Irreechaa in Minnesota
institutions.type: Cultural and spiritual festival and its organizing committee
institutions.location: Twin Cities, including Lake Nokomis (per MNopedia) and Powderhorn Park (2026) in Minneapolis
body: Once a year, in September, Oromos of the Twin Cities gather to sing, dance, eat and give thanks. MNopedia places the gathering at Lake Nokomis in Minneapolis; for 2026, the organizer’s listing and Oromo Diaspora Media place the September 19 event at Powderhorn Park, where the May 2 event was also held. The celebration is often described to Americans as "Oromo Thanksgiving." MNopedia notes that Ethiopia prohibited it for over a hundred years, and that violence at the October 2016 Irreechaa in Ethiopia killed 55 people by the government's count, or 700 by the count of others.

An October 2025 Ampers report describes gatherings in Minnesota in both May and September, run by a Minnesota-based Irreechaa organization with a board and volunteer committees. Talile Gobena, a volunteer on its marketing committee, called the festival a symbol of resilience, and board member Tolcha Gemechu said that wherever there are Oromos, even in small numbers, they still celebrate.
keyFacts: Held in the Twin Cities each September, at Lake Nokomis per MNopedia (the September 19, 2026 event was listed at Powderhorn Park); Ampers reports gatherings in May and September.
Prohibited in Ethiopia for over a hundred years, by MNopedia's account.
October 2016: Deadly violence at Irreechaa in Ethiopia, with 55 deaths by government count and 700 by others.

institutions.name: Multicultural Autism Action Network
body: The Multicultural Autism Action Network is a Minnesota nonprofit with roots among caregivers of autistic children from diverse communities who met obstacles to services first hand. It offers education, one-on-one and group family support, and legislative advocacy, and it trains schools, state agencies, law enforcement and health care providers. It serves multicultural communities and is not specific to Oromo families.

Its website offers videos in Oromo, Somali, Amharic and English. In October 2023 it held a family camp for autistic youth and their families from the Somali and Oromo communities, with the Autism Society of Minnesota. According to the University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration, it ran vaccination clinics for children with autism during the pandemic with health care partners. Executive director Maren Christenson Hofer told the institute she testified on about 20 state bills in one year, and Fatima Molas is a co-founder.
keyFacts: Videos in Oromo, Somali, Amharic and English.
October 2023: Family camp for Somali and Oromo families.
Trains schools, state agencies, law enforcement and health care providers.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions and describes no person or family. No study of how Oromo people in Minnesota understand disability was found. What follows comes from a small Minnesota survey that does not separate Oromo respondents, one study in the Oromia region of Ethiopia, and one Ethiopian training study with few Oromo participants. Oromo Minnesotans differ by faith, region, generation and time in the United States, and no research was found on how views vary across those lines.
questions: Which language do you want to use today, and do you want an interpreter who speaks Afaan Oromo fluently?
What words do you or your family use for this, and which words do you want us to use?
Would you like to tell me what you or your family think caused this, or would you rather not?
Who gave you a label, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open for you, and what do you want it to avoid?
Who do you want involved in this decision, and what do you want to decide for yourself?
Is faith or traditional healing part of your care, and how should services fit alongside it?
What do you want to know about who will see your information?
Would you like to meet other people or parents in your own language, or would you rather not?
Do you want written materials, and in which language and script, or would you rather hear this spoken?

context.heading: A Minnesota survey, without Oromo respondents separated
body: The Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities' 2017 survey, run by MarketResponse International, included 52 East African respondents. They were 62 percent Somalia-born, 35 percent Ethiopia-born and 4 percent Kenya-born. The report does not identify Oromo respondents, and a sample this small cannot speak for any one group.

In that sample, 73 percent agreed people with developmental disabilities should be encouraged to take part in the community and 71 percent agreed they should be allowed to vote. Twenty-four percent said they would be concerned if a person with a developmental disability moved into their neighborhood, and 20 percent said such people should not make major life decisions. Twenty-five percent agreed that the extra costs of raising a child with a developmental disability are the family's problem, compared with 3 percent of white respondents. The survey did not ask why.
Asked what mattered, 82 percent rated quality, coordinated health care as important, 80 percent legal advice and representation, and 78 percent programs connecting parents.

sources.label: Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities, 2017 Minnesota Racial and Ethnic Communities Survey

context.heading: A study in Oromia, Ethiopia
body: A 2015 Addis Ababa University thesis by Adugna Lema used interviews, observation and focus groups in Sebeta Hawas district, Oromia. The record does not state the sample size. It reports that local belief systems strongly shaped how disability was seen there, and that some religious teachings framed disabled people as cursed, sinful or linked to misfortune. It also reports barriers to school and health care, few disability-focused services, and the resilience of disabled people who had succeeded. It describes one district in Ethiopia and not Minnesota.

sources.label: Adugna Lema (2015), The Conception of Disability and Challenges of Person With Disability, Addis Ababa University

context.heading: An autism training study in Ethiopia
body: A 2021 study by Zeleke, Hughes and Kanyongo followed 34 educators and health professionals through a five-day workshop at the University of Gondar. Four identified as Oromo, and results were not reported by ethnicity. Some participants relied on traditional explanations of autism during the training. Participants rated their own agencies' outreach to places of worship, clergy and Indigenous religious leaders as below average, at 1.9 on a 1 to 4 scale. Knowledge scores rose after the training, but the authors note a self-made test, no follow-up and no real patients.

sources.label: Zeleke, Hughes and Kanyongo (2021), Frontiers in Psychiatry

context.heading: Language and what could not be found
body: Confirm that an interpreter is fluent in Afaan Oromo and not only from the same country, and ask the person what language they prefer. The Multicultural Autism Action Network has videos in Oromo. Explain plainly that disability services are a right and how information is kept private, and check understanding at each step.

No verified source was found for Afaan Oromo words for disability, for stigmatizing terms or for preferred terms, so ask a qualified interpreter and the person. No Oromo-specific Minnesota research was found on fear of systems, immigration concerns or trust, which is no reason to assume those barriers or to rule them out. No source was found on Oromo-specific roles for elders, extended family or gender in disability caregiving. A published profile of an Oromo disabled leader or self-advocate could not be confirmed either, which says something about what has been written and nothing about whether such leaders exist.

organizations.intro: MNopedia calls the Twin Cities "Little Oromia" and says Minnesota's Oromo population is the largest outside Ethiopia and Kenya. It also says no census gives an accurate count, and that an estimate of tens of thousands in the Twin Cities area would not be far off. Since the 1980s Oromo Minnesotans have organized through mutual aid, a community center, mosques and churches, sports and media. The list below is starting points for learning. It is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Oromo Sports Federation in North America
entries.location: North America, with its tournament in the Twin Cities
entries.purpose: Runs a one-week annual tournament in the Twin Cities in late July or early August, with youth teams from other North American cities. MNopedia says St. Paul first hosted in 2011, and both mayors declared it Oromo Week; the federation’s own history puts its first tournament in Toronto in 1996, with a Minnesota club among six. Oromo Diaspora Media covered the 2026 event in Minnesota.
entries.linkLabel: Oromo Diaspora Media on the 2026 tournament

entries.name: Tawfiq Islamic Center
entries.purpose: Opened in 2004 as Masjid Tawfiq, which MNopedia calls the first Oromo mosque in North America, and renamed in 2006. Oromo Diaspora Media lists it as a partner.
entries.linkLabel: Ampers segment on Little Oromia, which names the center

entries.name: Bilal Oromo Dawa Center
entries.purpose: A Muslim community center serving the Oromo community in Fridley and nearby cities, with a madrasa and Qur'an learning.

entries.name: Our Redeemer Oromo Evangelical Church of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Grew from a Bible study group into a church in 1993. Holds Sunday services in person and online, a children's service, and weekly programs.

entries.name: Abenezer Oromo Evangelical Church
entries.location: Twin Cities; no published address could be found
entries.purpose: An Oromo Evangelical congregation listed as a partner by Oromo Diaspora Media.

entries.name: Oromo-American Citizens Council
entries.purpose: A registered nonprofit in the civil rights and advocacy category. Its latest federal filing, for 2024, is the short form for small organizations. No website or recent public program activity was found.

entries.name: Oromo Legacy Leadership & Advocacy Association
entries.purpose: A nonprofit serving the socio-cultural needs of Oromo people worldwide. It publishes reports on human rights in Ethiopia, the most recent featured on its home page dated 2023.

entries.name: Oromia Global Forum
entries.purpose: An August 2026 article in the Journal of Oromo Studies describes it as linking civic, professional, faith-based and human-rights actors across several continents. No official website could be found.

entries.name: Ethiopian Sports Federation in North America
entries.purpose: An Ethiopian, not Oromo-specific, body. Its 43rd annual soccer tournament ran June 27 to July 4, 2026, in the Twin Cities, with organizers expecting more than 20,000 people. Not to be confused with the Oromo Sports Federation.

entries.name: Oromo Diaspora Media
entries.purpose: Describes itself as an independent, nonpartisan nonprofit news organization covering Oromo diaspora life. Its listed partners include the Minnesota Department of Human Services, the Minnesota Department of Health and Hennepin County. Latest post when checked: October 8, 2026.

entries.name: Oromia Media Network
entries.type: Television and online, in Afaan Oromoo, English and Amharic
entries.location: St. Paul, 1437 Marshall Avenue, per its nonprofit record
entries.purpose: A nonprofit network formed in 2014, covering Oromia and Ethiopia. Its latest federal filing, for 2024, shows revenue of $213,558. The link goes to its nonprofit record because the web address carrying its name now shows unrelated advertising.

entries.name: Voice of Oromiyaa
entries.purpose: A weekly Oromo program on KFAI, on the schedule for Sundays from 5 to 6 p.m.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers Minnesota immigrants and communities of color and has an "Oromo in Minnesota" section. Multicultural, not specific to Oromo Minnesotans.

entries.name: VOA Afaan Oromoo
entries.purpose: Voice of America's service for Afaan Oromoo speakers. The site was up when checked, with no suspension notice. Al Jazeera reported in October 2025 that VOA as a whole has run on a limited basis since most staff were placed on leave in March 2025.

entries.name: BBC News Afaan Oromoo
entries.purpose: News in Afaan Oromoo, available online and on Facebook since September 2017, with shortwave radio planned to follow.

entries.name: Oromia Broadcasting Network
entries.location: Adama, Oromia, Ethiopia, by its own materials
entries.purpose: The Oromia regional public broadcaster, funded by the regional government. Afaan Oromo is its main language, with programming in 17 Ethiopian languages plus English, Arabic and French.
